summaries.example: Imagine two children whose brains and bodies are exactly alike. One lives where the word “water” means ordinary water. The other lives on a planet where the same-looking liquid is made of different stuff. Their thoughts connected to “water” may still differ because their surroundings differ. A different example is a notebook: a child may use it to remember where a museum is. Philosophers ask whether the notebook is only a helpful tool or partly part of the remembering process.
summaries.summary: Externalism is a family of views about the mind. It says that the body and brain do not always tell the whole story about a person’s mental life. Content externalism says that what a thought means can depend on the natural world or on a language community. Extended-mind theories make a stronger and different claim: some thinking processes or parts that carry thought may reach beyond the body. The article discusses famous imaginary cases, such as a duplicate person on a planet with a different liquid called “water,” and a person who uses a notebook to remember information. It also explains objections. Some philosophers think these cases show that the environment helps determine thought. Others say the cases show only that the environment supports thinking, not that it becomes part of the mind. The article also considers whether there can be a kind of “narrow” content shared by identical thinkers in different surroundings.
key_ideas: Some thoughts depend partly on a person’s surroundings, not only on the brain.
A community’s shared use of words can help shape what someone means.
Content externalism and the extended mind are different ideas: one concerns what thoughts mean, and the other concerns what carries or helps make thought happen.
Philosophers disagree about whether outside tools are parts of thinking or merely useful supports.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic changes how we picture the mind. It suggests that language, surroundings, tools, and social practices may matter to thinking. It also raises questions about memory, self-knowledge, and how actions are explained. Learning about the debate helps us notice that a helpful connection is not automatically the same as being a part of something.

important_terms.definition: The view that what happens in the mind is not always fixed only by what happens inside the body and brain.
The idea that the meaning or subject of a thought can depend partly on the world or on other people’s language.
The idea that some thinking may partly include things outside the body, such as using a notebook.
The part of a thought that tells what it is about, such as water in a thought about water.

questions_to_think_about: If two people have identical brains but live in different worlds, must they have exactly the same thoughts?
Is a notebook part of remembering, or is it only a tool for remembering?
How much do other people help give our words their meanings?

summaries.example: Consider a person who keeps a notebook containing a museum’s address. When planning a visit, she consults the notebook, reads the entry, and follows the directions. One interpretation says the notebook stores information that remains outside her mind but supports her memory. A state-oriented extended-mind view says the notebook entry may itself function as one of her beliefs. A process-oriented view instead says that the remembering includes the coordinated activity of her brain, eyes, hands, and notebook, without identifying a belief with the written sentence.
summaries.summary: Externalism about the mind denies that mental life is always completely determined by events inside the organism. The entry distinguishes two principal forms. Content externalism concerns the individuation of mental content: in some cases, what a person thinks depends on relations to a natural environment or a linguistic community. Putnam’s Twin Earth and Burge’s arthritis cases are designed to show that internal duplicates may differ in what they think, even when their behavior and inner histories are held fixed. The conclusion concerns dependence and individuation, not the claim that thoughts are literally located outside the body. Extended mind, by contrast, concerns the vehicles of content—the structures or processes that carry it. The canonical notebook case can be interpreted as an external belief-like state or as a larger remembering process involving active manipulation of the notebook. Critics distinguish constitution from mere coupling, question whether written symbols possess original intentionality, and ask how cognition should be identified. The article also examines narrow-content proposals, self-knowledge, mental causation, and relations among embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended approaches.
key_ideas: Putnam’s Twin Earth case argues that physically identical thinkers can have different thought contents when their natural environments differ.
Burge’s arthritis case argues that linguistic practices can help determine the concepts and beliefs a thinker possesses.
External individuation does not imply external location: a mental state may depend on the environment while still occurring in the person.
The extended-mind thesis concerns the vehicles or bearers of content, not merely the content itself, and is logically independent of content externalism.
The notebook case motivates state-oriented and process-oriented versions of extended mind, but critics argue that it may show only embedding or causal support.
Responses include rejecting the thought experiments, questioning intuition-based methods, defending narrow content, and disputing whether the internal/external distinction is well defined.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate bears on what counts as a mental state, how concepts acquire meaning, and whether psychological explanation can be individualistic. It also affects theories of mind-body relations, the causal explanation of action, and the status of tools and social practices in cognition. Its importance lies partly in its distinctions: environmental dependence need not mean external location, and dependence or cooperation with a tool need not mean that the tool constitutes a mental state.

important_terms.definition: The general thesis that bodily and neural facts do not always, by themselves, determine all of a person’s mental occurrences.
The view that at least some mental states are individuated partly by relations to objects, properties, facts, or practices outside the individual’s biological boundaries.
Dependence of what a state is, as a state of a certain kind, on relations to things distinct from that state.
The view that some mental vehicles—physical or computational bearers of content—are partly constituted by factors outside the organism.
Content understood as dependent on the thinker’s environment, including natural and social surroundings.
A proposed kind of content that would remain shared by thinkers with the same internal condition across different contexts.
The property of being about something; thoughts, beliefs, desires, and intentions commonly have this feature.
A relation of dependence or interaction with an outside structure that does not by itself show that the structure is part of the mental process.

questions_to_think_about: Does a difference in reference or truth-conditions necessarily imply a difference in the thinker’s mental state?
Can a notebook entry have the same functional role as a belief without itself being a belief?
What would distinguish a cognitive process that is extended from one that is merely supported by its surroundings?
Could a person know the content of a thought immediately if that content depends partly on the environment?
Is narrow content genuine content, or is it only a description of internal processing?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya and her exact physical duplicate both say, “The lake contains water.” Maya lives on Earth, where the clear liquid is H2O. Her duplicate lives on Twin Earth, where the liquid looks and behaves the same but has a different chemical structure. Even if everything inside their bodies matches, the two statements may mean different things because their environments differ. Now imagine Maya uses a notebook to remember an address. Is the notebook just an outside aid, or is the remembering partly made from Maya’s brain activity plus her actions with the notebook? Philosophers give different answers.
summaries.summary: Externalism about the mind says that inner events do not always settle everything about mental life. Content externalism focuses on what thoughts mean. In the Twin Earth example, a person and a molecule-for-molecule duplicate live in environments containing different substances called “water.” Their inner states match, but their thoughts may concern different things. In Burge’s language-based case, the meaning of a person’s belief changes when the surrounding community uses a word differently. These cases support the idea that mental content can depend on natural or social surroundings. The entry separates this from the extended-mind thesis. Extended mind says that some vehicles of thought—such as a structure carrying information or a process using it—may partly lie beyond the body. A notebook might be an external belief, or it might be a tool used in a larger remembering activity. Critics say the notebook may be merely embedded in cognition, and they question whether written words have their own original meaning. The discussion also considers narrow content, which is meant to capture what identical thinkers share, and broader consequences for self-knowledge and explanations of action.
key_ideas: A person’s surroundings may help determine what a word or thought means.
A shared language community can matter just as a physical environment can.
Externalism about content and the extended mind make different claims and do not automatically come together.
A mental state can depend on the outside world without being located outside the body.
Critics argue that thought experiments may not prove externalism and that outside tools may support thinking without becoming parts of the mind.
Some philosophers try to preserve narrow content that identical thinkers would share, while others doubt that this can be done.
summaries.why_it_matters: Externalism connects everyday questions about language and memory with deep questions about the mind. It asks whether thinking is something that happens only inside a person or also depends on relationships with the world and other people. The debate can help explain why tools, customs, and surroundings matter while still allowing us to ask whether they are genuine parts of cognition.

important_terms.definition: The view that the mind is not always completely determined by what happens inside the body and brain.
The view that some thought contents depend partly on the thinker’s environment or language community.
The meaning or subject of a thought, belief, desire, or other mental state.
The idea that what a mental state is depends partly on its relations to things outside the thinker.
The view that some thinking states or processes partly include outside structures or activities.
The idea that an outside object helps a mental process without necessarily being a part of that process.
A proposed kind of content determined by what is shared inside the thinker, rather than by the whole environment.

questions_to_think_about: Would Maya and her duplicate have different beliefs if their inner lives were exactly alike?
Does using a calculator make the calculator part of your thinking? Why or why not?
Can a word’s meaning depend on how a community uses it?
What is the difference between a tool helping a thought and a tool being part of the thought?
Could a person know what they are thinking without checking the world around them?
